TechnologyTab.title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
TechnologyTab.text:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side programming language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.

Governments and cyber-security agencies rushed to contain the fallout, urging website owners to check if their sites were affected and, if so, install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.

But in the days since the issues came to light, disruption to sites and services has continued to ripple around the world.

Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.

It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server.

Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites.

When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.

It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.

According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.

It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, external, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity".

A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.

Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws were inherent in the language itself, affecting versions of PHP released over the last decade.

The technical bugs, given the technical IDs CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were ranked a 9.2 out of 10 in severity by researchers.

Calif researcher Ryan Austin, who helped uncover it, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found".

Wiz wrote in a blog post, external about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the bugs to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.

AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.

He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.

Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.

The alert on 21 October disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.

It included Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.

Sites and pages were also taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and some BBC pages, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website on Wednesday.

But while many sites were back up by Thursday, others were still being taken down temporarily elsewhere as people and businesses check for potential exposure.

The UK Government revealed on Thursday some "limited" services may be offline temporarily.

It said 32 sites had been taken down as a precaution, none of them large public-facing services.

In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

On Friday, local media in Japan reported telecom operator SoftBank Corp had temporarily suspended emergency alerts for earthquakes, tsunamis and other disasters.

According to the Mainichi newspaper, external, SoftBank customers have been urged to make sure they have other ways to get alerts about natural disasters - with its mobile phone alerts not set to sound even in the event of a strong earthquake.

The service is reportedly set to resume on Monday.

Some experts warn the issue could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.

More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, said cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere of UNSW Sydney.

The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.

Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations, external that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.

"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP in posts on X.

Tech companies also sought to quickly secure their systems.

E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue, but its websites were operating as normal.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, also said it had seen "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, external.

As of Friday morning, no successful attacks had been reported.

But experts have warned any impact may take time to become fully apparent.

And operators of a number of services where PHP may have been used - not just in web development - are still being urged to check their systems and implement updates, where necessary.

"It is important to remember that PHP is not limited to web applications," said Daniel Stewart, head of threat intelligence at global risk manager LRQA.

"It is commonly found in the management interfaces of network appliances, load balancers, and embedded devices, which are often overlooked during these incidents."

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches has climbed - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.

The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action.

But small businesses with sites, including those built using WordPress, may be wondering how to protect themselves.

Those who own websites or manage infrastructure running PHP have been urged to secure their websites by updating to the latest version.

Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update".

If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.

If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied".

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends, external considering temporarily taking sites offline if updates or temporary protections cannot be applied quickly enough.

The US National Security Agency has also urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks, telling people to closely monitor updates from software vendors.

"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.

And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.
TechnologyTab.description: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side programming language used in web development...

TechnologyTab.title: 'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber security scramble
TechnologyTab.text:
Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".

Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse.

"It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.

He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites.

"The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said.

"Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."

PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.

But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.

Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.

In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP.

"Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.

He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.

Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts.

"Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said.

"But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."

The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.

Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.

"It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.

The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.

But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real.

"We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.

He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating.

"This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.

He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.

As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.

One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.

In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.

It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.

AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.

The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.

But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it.

"We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.

He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks"....

TechnologyTab.title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
TechnologyTab.text:
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.

But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.

The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.

"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."

He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.

"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.

He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.

Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.

That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.

Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.

"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.

His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.

"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.

Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.

"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."

But his customers are getting more demanding.

"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.

"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."

And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.

Why is such data so important?

If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.

Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.

"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.

And until recently, that data was not available.

"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.

At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.

"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."

TechnologyTab.title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
TechnologyTab.text:
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.

The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.

The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.

He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.

California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.

The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.

Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.

Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.

It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.

In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.

Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.

Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.

The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.

Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."

The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.

After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.

Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.

Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.

With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.

Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.

Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.

It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.

And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.

The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.

Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

TechnologyTab.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
TechnologyTab.text:
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.

Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.

There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.

Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.

"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.

She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".

The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".

"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.

Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".

"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.

But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.

He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.

Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.

"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.

"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."

Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.

He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.

"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.

He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.

PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.

It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.

When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.

It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.

According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.

And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.

Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.

Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end...

TechnologyTab.title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
TechnologyTab.text:
I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.

We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction.

In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building.

The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet.

There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025.

But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution.

Less than two months ago, 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI.

It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant.

The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit.

One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult.

However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI.

The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix.

It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked.

From that point the clock started ticking.

As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site.

"There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University.

"How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers?

"Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."

But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made.

We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either.

As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success.

Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story.

"We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4.

"We have enormous capability to handle these risks."

But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in.

Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first.

For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee.

EntertainmentTab.title: Mitchell Lawrie, 15, eyes £501,000 live TV win over Luke Littler
EntertainmentTab.text:
At just 15 years old, Mitchell Lawrie has his sights on a £501,000 bullseye should he beat world darts champion Luke Littler in a potentially life-changing live appearance on national television.

The Renfrew teenager is one of 24 amateur players chosen to take part in Netflix's live special, Beat Luke Littler, which will be broadcast from the Manchester Central Convention Complex on Friday.

Each contestant has the chance to face Littler in a single leg of 501 but the first to beat the 19-year-old two-time world champion will land the big-money prize and bring the competition to an immediate end.

"If someone has already beaten Littler, that's the show done," Lawrie told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

He added: "There's a bundle of good players in there and you're just hoping you get a chance before they get a chance. There's a few big names I want to go before."

Lawrie admits "there's going to be nerves there obviously" and "being live on Netflix at 15 years of age is just something else".

However, he points out: "Everybody there has a chance at the end of the day.

"He is obviously the best player in the world so it may be only one leg of darts but it is a very hard leg to win."

Nevertheless, Lawrie already has a victory over Littler under his belt.

"It was at the World Cup junior darts in Gibraltar in 2023, Scotland against England and we beat the team that Luke Littler was in," he recalls.

"We beat them 4-3 in a deciding leg and it's one of those memories that sticks with you forever.

"We also went on to win that tournament. It is the first time Scotland ever won the World Cup and it was my first year - it was something else.

"It was a surreal experience that I would love to have back."

Indeed, Lawrie was crowned WDF Open Youth World Champion last year before being described as "the future of darts" by Jimmy van Schie after the Dutchman beat the Scot when he became the first teenager to reach the WDF World Championship final in December.

Lawrie, whose inspiration is former world number one Gary Anderson, twice winner of the more prestigious PDC World Darts Championship, says he has been playing darts since his grandfather mounted a board on a chair when he was two years old.

"It just spiralled from there," he says. "But I never took it seriously until three and a half years ago.

"People still want to be a professional footballer, and it was the same for me, but I realised at a young age I wasn't good enough for it so I had to do something else and I just chose darts and I stuck to it and turned out quite good at it."

EntertainmentTab.title: Meghan to co-host Junior MasterChef Australia
EntertainmentTab.text:
The Duchess of Sussex has been confirmed as a co-hostof the new season of Junior MasterChef Australia.

Meghan will join the 2027 series as a "special guest" with fellow host Poh Ling Yeow, according to Australia's Channel 10.

The duchess said she "can't wait" to take part in the programme after an appearance as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia last year. It was the show's largest Sunday audience since 2023, according to the statement from Paramount ANZ.

The announcement comes as Meghan faces increased scrutiny due to her father Thomas Markle being accused of child sexual abuse. He denies the allegations.

The BBC understands Meghan broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and authorities knew he had abused young girls.

Markle has strongly rejected the accusations as "lies" which are being used to destroy his reputation.

Meghan's return to Australia follows a four-day tour of the country she and Prince Harry undertook in April.

Meghan's MasterChef debut was announced on the second day of the tour, a Wednesday on which the duchess had been notably absent from public-facing appearances. That evening, it was revealed she had been filming an episode of the programme.

It is understood she was not paid for her appearance. Australia's Network 10, which airs the series as part of Paramount ANZ, did not respond to a question from the BBC about whether Meghan would be paid for co-hosting the Junior MasterChef season.

"I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun," Meghan said in a statement.

In August, the Sussexes announced they were moving back to the UK from California. The couple left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.

They embarked on media careers which included a high-profile interview with Oprah Winfrey and a deal with Netflix and Spotify.

Meghan's lifestyle and cookery show on Netflix, With Love, Meghan, ran for two series and a Christmas special but did not perform well with audiences.

She also launched lifestyle brand As Ever, which includes a food range, but in March it ended its partnership with the streaming platform.

Last year her trademark was registered in more than a dozen product categories in Australia, including cookware and table linen.

EntertainmentTab.title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation
EntertainmentTab.text:
The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.

The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.

Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027.

However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".

NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.

"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.

"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."

NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".

Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.

"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."

Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

EntertainmentTab.title: Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears
EntertainmentTab.text:
A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".

The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.

They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".

The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".

He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."

Nicklin will not determine the truth or accuracy of the allegations, only whether they can be published.

He also urged the press and public not to speculate about the identity of the man, who is referred to in court as PPT.

"The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings," he said.

"Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact."

Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court that any publication "would have a potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life."

She said the man had made a suicide attempt after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his response to the allegations, and later absconded from hospital and attempted suicide for a second time.

She added in written submissions: "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur.

"The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple - now more than 10 - doctors."

Mansoori also said the man "has no intention of returning to public life".

Gavin Millar KC, for ITN and GNM, said in written submissions that "numerous allegations" had been gathered during "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a "strong" public interest in publishing them.

He said reporters had spoken to more than 100 people, and that the resulting allegations "indicated a pattern of behaviour".

Millar later said many of the women "have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result".

He added that while the state may have a responsibility to protect life, applying that principle to this case would require the state to intervene in "lawful journalistic activities" to prevent "an autonomous act by the claimant himself".

The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

EntertainmentTab.title: Russell Brand told police he never had non-consensual sex
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand told police in interviews in response to allegations of rape and sexual assault that he had been "very promiscuous" in the past, but had never engaged in "non-consensual sexual activity", a court has heard.

Brand, 51, was interviewed four times between 2023 and 2025 by officers.

The TV and media personality is currently on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London on three counts of rape and other offences. He denies all the charges.

Jurors heard on Tuesday that he gave a prepared statement in each of the police interviews. In November 2023, he said: "I have repeatedly stated publicly and written extensively that I led a very promiscuous life, that I have spent years openly denouncing. I have never engaged in non-consensual activity."

Brand went on to say the allegations were made in "a defamatory and fictitious documentary", which he said contained "false and anonymised" interviews.

He added that "subsequently both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which has resulted in further encounters to be invented or reimagined".

In court on Tuesday, the jury was also asked formally to find Brand not guilty of a charge of indecent assault.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said there was "insufficient evidence to support the charge of indecent assault".

This charge related to a woman who said Brand grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into a toilet in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

The jury was then given an amended indictment, which charges Brand with attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

The prosecution will conclude on Wednesday morning before the defence is expected to start.

Brand denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

EntertainmentTab.title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
EntertainmentTab.text:
Busted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".

The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.

He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.

James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.

"Wow, what the hell happened?" James wrote on Monday. "One minute you're heading out on tour, the next thing you know you're on the bench and out of the game.

"My condition was serious and the doctors told me I had a few years left to live.

"I'm happy to share now that my youngest brother, Chris, who stepped in for me on tour last year, has saved my life yet again. This time quite literally by donating me one of his kidneys."

EntertainmentTab.title: Ash Dykes completes Congo Basin expedition after going 'missing' for 24 hours
EntertainmentTab.text:
An adventurer has completed the first leg of his latest challenge after losing contact with his UK team for almost 24 hours.

Ash Dykes, 35, from Old Colwyn, Conwy, holds five world records but his most recent quest was the first of six back-to-back expeditions he will take on in extreme environments.

Dykes encountered elephants, gorillas and was chased by "killer" bees as he rowed more than 434 miles (700 km) along rivers in the Congo Basin, central Africa.

Towards the end of the journey, Dykes' portable satellite kit lost power. He said: "My parents and fiancée were worrying but as soon as I had a bit of signal I made sure I got in touch".

In his latest Project 6 challenge, Dykes will attempt six expeditions in very different locations.

He has previously walked 4,000-miles (6,437km) along the length of China's Yangtze River in 2019 and kayaked the length of the Coppename river in Suriname from source to sea in 37 days

On "going missing", Dykes said his "power bank just shut down".

"We were underneath the jungle canopy, because we were staying with a small community, and then it took me about 20 hours before I could get out the first message," he said.

As the adventurer is sharing expeditions "live", he said he had learned lessons from the experience going forward.

He said: "I don't think the world's ready for a truly live expedition so I've learned from that...

"If I lose contact again with the team, we have to keep it within the team because I do know that that hit alarms and a lot of people were stressed and panicked. So it's important to make this as live as possible, but moving forward, it can't be that live anymore."

During the adventure, Dykes said his biggest fear was not the danger posed by wildlife or disease, but the extreme heat during many hours of kayaking in rivers home to crocodiles and hippos with no shade.

He said: "We took the warnings seriously. Experience means listening to local advice, reading the conditions and making the decisions that get your team through safely."

For the explorer, the main highlight was spending time with the Baka tribe, a semi-nomadic indigenous ethnic group.

They demonstrated their hunting prowess which involves trapping animals in netting set up around the jungle.

"They were amazing, they took us under their wings, they showed us how they survive, how they hunt, how they gather," Dykes said.

"They took us to an area where we saw a group of gorillas within Sanga National Park. I was about five metres away from silverback."

Dykes was joined on his trek by local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire as well as videographer Will Perez, who has been helping chart the journey with regular social media posts.

His popularity on TikTok has soared following his latest adventure.

Dykes said: "It felt like the world was on the river with us."

But he added some followers were disappointed in the lack of drama.

"Everyone wanted that excitement, that danger, but if something was to happen, I'd be criticised: 'this is dangerous'.

"Now that I've made it unscathed, everyone's like: 'It's easy, there were no crocs'.

"So there's no true winning when you go that viral."

He said he lost 11lbs (5kg) during the trip, as he was relying mostly on ration packs of food.

In a social media post to mark the end of the first stage of Project 6, Dykes said: "It's been a lot. We've faced ups and downs - seen some crazy wildlife, but more importantly we've survived."

Dykes said he would reveal the second stage of Project 6 next week, and hinted it would be somewhere "a lot colder" than the Congo Basin.

EntertainmentTab.title: A Court of Splintered Harmony: Fans revel in midnight release at Carrickfergus event
EntertainmentTab.text:
Torrential rain and high winds may not be what many would consider fantastical.

But it didn't stop about 30 hardcore fans turning out for the latest release of author Sarah J Maas’ romantasy series, A Court of Splintered Harmony, in Carrickfergus, County Antrim.

The sixth book in Maas's multi-million book selling series, A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR), was released at midnight on Tuesday after a five-year wait.

On Monday evening, a midnight release event was held in The Secret Bookshelf, an independent bookshop just off the town's main street.

Friends Katie Mccabrey and Amy Savage were among those who went along to try and get one of the first copies when the embargo broke.

Like many others, Katie and Amy love reading books as a way to unwind from the stresses and pressures of every day life.

"I just love reading these kinds of fantasy books because the real world is a little bit terrible and I love to escape into a fantasyland of fairies and anything other worldly," Amy says.

"We're all here tonight because we all share just needing to escape from everyday life in common and this is a great way to do it," Katie adds.

Among the activities lined up at The Secret Bookshelf to distract excited fans from clock-watching are felting, friendship bracelet making and a dedicated fan-chat area for readers to discuss their theories.

Some attending opt for comfy clothing, sporting pyjamas and slippers as they waited for the midnight drop.

The wait has almost been too much for Katie.

"I couldn't sleep, I've been so excited - I've been hyped up for two weeks straight," she says.

"I'm actually halfway through another book that I couldn't pay attention to because I've been so busy thinking about the characters from ACOTAR," Amy jokes.

"So I'm going to have to go back and re-read the book that I'm 300 pages deep in because I've been so busy and so excited for this new launch."

For those whose social media algorithms do not revolve around "BookTok", the literary discussion side of TikTok, A Court of Thorns and Roses - or ACOTAR for short - is a fantasy romance series, which gets its name from the first book.

It's set in the fictional world of Prythian, and without spoiling the now six-book series, fans have flocked to the story in their droves to read about the protagonist's dealings with love and the fae.

Maas is also credited with fuelling interest in the romantasy genre, which has skyrocketed in popularity due to its discussion on social media.

There have been five books published so far:

A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015)

A Court of Mist and Fury (2016)

A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017)

A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018)

A Court of Silver Flames (2021)

Monday's midnight release event is the brainchild of Jo Zebedee, who runs The Secret Bookshelf alongside her husband, Chris.

Harkening back to her time helping to run the midnight launches of the Harry Potter books, Jo decided to bring the same magic for fans of the much loved romantasy series.

"We are a big fantasy shop, I'm a fantasy, sci-fi writer so it's in my blood, so we very much celebrate the world's that sometime can be difficult to find a space in mainstream books," she explains.

"There's something around the excitement of books and just that whole vibe of here's something to really celebrate.. we just wanted to bring that all together to make a fun night."

Jo enlisted the help of not only local crafters for the event, but local businesses who gifted attendees treats for the late night.

She thinks its the place of independent bookshops, like hers, to foster the excitement amongst young people for reading.

"I think events is when a bookshop comes to life," she says.

"It's about a love of books and tonight is just such a love of books."

EntertainmentTab.title: Super Bowl 2027: Jay-Z to perform at half-time show
EntertainmentTab.text:
Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL has announced.

Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in selecting each year's performer but he has not performed before at the NFL championship game.

"Anticipation as to who Jay-Z might have guest star at halftime for the big game will now kick off," the NFL said in a statement. "Of course, his wife, Beyoncé, will be atop the list."

Next year's Super Bowl LXI will take place on 14 February near Los Angeles.

The hip-hop star will follow in the footsteps of other recent half-time performers including Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Usher, Rihanna and The Weeknd.

The musical performance draws global attention while the sport is watched by tens of millions of people in the US.

Kendrick Lamar's 2025 performance was the most watched Super Bowl half-time show in history and won the Emmy award for outstanding music direction.

The announcement was made after Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter, performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played.

The LA shows were part of a tour to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt.

"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," said Jay-Z.

"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he "couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring".

"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said.

The star's accolades include being the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, 25 Grammy awards and being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

EntertainmentTab.title: Shopkeeper in Catford immortalised by royal portrait artist
EntertainmentTab.text:
A corner shop owner from south London has been painted by a royal portraitist in a project to recognise the impact of independent businesses in their local communities.

Artist Nick Bashall, who painted Princess Anne, has depicted Kaual Patel, owner of Torridon Convenience Store in Catford.

The work will be revealed to the public in a new exhibition, Local Royalty, alongside paintings by other royal artists of pub, cafe and takeaway owners.

The event was inspired by research that indicated nearly 80% of the public believed independent businesses such as corner shops are underappreciated.

The exhibition depicts Patel alongside three other small business owners who have been immortalised in a manner historically reserved for royalty, titans of industry and stars of stage and screen.

He took over the shop from his father and uncle and has spent the past two decades creating a hub for the local community and championing local producers.

"The days I spent being painted by Nick, live in the shop, were unforgettable, but what made it truly special was seeing it through the eyes of my customers," said Patel.

EntertainmentTab.title: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90
EntertainmentTab.text:
Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.

The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise, from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.

In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.

His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes, external on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."

Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."

They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".

Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk.

Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.

He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.

His big break came as the capable, loyal and sincere young Chekov, who often proudly claimed that everything originated in Russia, a running gag that amused the crew and audiences alike.

The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut.

But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.

The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.

Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter., external

He was arguably more integral to the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

Koenig's seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a Next Generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in the modern series Star Trek: Picard in 2023.

He also wrote an episode of the original show's animated series spin-off, in 1973, titled The Infinite Vulcan.

EntertainmentTab.title: Sir Tom Jones 'truly sorry' as he cancels concerts due to illness
EntertainmentTab.text:
Sir Tom Jones said he is "truly sorry" after rescheduling two forthcoming concerts due to "a bad case of the flu".

The 86-year-old singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, is currently on his Come Gather Round world tour.

He announced the decision to push back his Monday show in Los Angeles, and Tuesday's concert in San Diego, following doctor's advice.

In a post on Instagram, he wrote: "Following doctor's advice, I unfortunately have to reschedule tonight's show in Los Angeles and tomorrow's show in San Diego."

The San Diego concert will now take place at The Rady Shell, at Jacobs Park, on 3 November, while his Los Angeles show has been moved to 4 November.

On Instagram, he wrote: "I've had a great time these last few weeks, completing 20 shows and singing for wonderful audiences across the USA, but unexpectedly I've been hit with a bad case of the flu."

He added: "I'm truly sorry for any inconvenience caused. I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"All tickets for the original dates will remain valid. However, if customers are unable to attend the rescheduled dates, they are advised to contact their original point of purchase for a refund."

The post was shared just hours before he was expected to perform at the Greek Theatre, with the Los Angeles venue among those wishing Sir Tom well.

The It's Not Unusual and What's New Pussycat? singer recently made headlines after revealing ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from The Voice UK coaching panel.

Sir Tom, who has served as an on-off coach on the popular singing competition since its 2012 debut, shared the news on Instagram last month, amid speculation he had been "dropped" from its 2027 series.

The Delilah and She's A Lady singer has achieved three UK number one singles and four chart-topping albums during a music career spanning more than six decades.

His awards include one Grammy, two Brits and an Ivor Novello; Sir Tom also received a knighthood from the late Queen Elizabeth II in 2006 for his services to music.

GeneralTab.title: Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner in pivotal general election
GeneralTab.text:
Exit polls suggest there is no clear winner of Israel's pivotal general election, with neither veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on track to secure a majority.

Two Israeli broadcasters projected that Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his "Change Bloc" would win 51 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, as would Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies. A third broadcaster's poll gave Netanyahu a lead of three seats.

Much will depend on the role played by the two Arab parties, which were projected to win a record 18 or 19 seats.

Voter turnout on Tuesday was the highest in decades.

It stood at 77.7% when polls closed at 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT), which was the highest at that hour since 1999, the Central Elections Committee said.

Official results will start to be published overnight, but an estimated 600,000 absentee ballots cast mostly by military personnel - around 10% of the total number of votes - will not be fully counted until Thursday.

Once the final results are confirmed, and following consultations with all the political factions, Israel's president will invite the party leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a governing coalition - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

At the headquarters of Eisenkot's Yashar party in Tel Aviv, his supporters cheered and chanted "Bibi, go home!" after the initial exit polls published by public broadcaster Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13 projected that his bloc would emerge as the biggest in the Knesset, with between 52 and 53 seats, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's governing coalition.

Eisenkot said they had "made history" and promised to "ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israel's citizens".

His ally in the Beyachad party, former prime minister Yair Lapid, said Netanyahu's bloc had suffered a "crushing defeat".

However, there was no sign of surrender at the Jerusalem headquarters of Netanyahu's Likud party, which was projected to be the largest party in parliament.

Supporters there told the BBC that they were nervous. "It's not over until it's over, but I'm sweating," Itzik said.

Netanyahu's ally, Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, said celebrations on the left were "premature", while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told supporters of his far-right Jewish Power party to pray that the final results would lead to a "full-on right-wing government".

In the early hours of Wednesday, the broadcasters updated their exit polls. Kan and Channel 13's projections showed the blocs tied on 51 seats, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu's bloc 52 seats and Eisenkot's 49.

Later, Netanyahu appeared at Likud's headquarters and declared in a speech that his right-wing bloc had a "great majority". He also called for the formation of "a strong, right-wing national government".

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - were projected to win several extra seats in parliament following a reportedly strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

They are emerging as the kingmakers in the election, but only one party has openly backed working with them in government.

"I hope that the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats," United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas said.

After the 2021 elections, Abbas's party was part of a governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, which lasted a year before collapsing.

The chairman of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, warned that the grouping "cannot be ignored under any political scenario".

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, how to share the growing burden of military service, judicial reforms, and Israel's international standing.

Outside a polling station in an opposition stronghold in northern Tel Aviv, campaigners young and old were out in force, using every last moment to win that extra vote.

Zivit Abramson, 88, told the BBC that she had voted for Eisenkot because Netanyahu was "ruining this country". "He's all about himself, only about himself," she added.

Elsewhere, Claire Tugendhaft said she had voted for Netanyahu "because I think he's the best man in the country to lead the country towards the outside world".

The prime minister and his government allies urged their supporters to head to the polls with warnings about a surge in turnout among left-wing and Arab voters.

"If you don't vote, we'll wake up tomorrow with a left-wing government, Arab parties, extreme Islam, and we'll lose the country," Netanyahu was filmed saying.

Likud and several other right-wing parties asked for voting hours to be extended beyond 22:00 local time - a move many of their opponents saw as a sign of growing desperation.

The Central Elections Committee ultimately rejected their request, saying that "the current circumstances do not justify an extension" and that the high turnout "reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process".

GeneralTab.title: Bahamas: King Charles acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
GeneralTab.text:
King Charles has arrived in the Bahamas for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean - the first time he has visited the region as monarch.

The King, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was given a ceremonial welcome at the airport before attending a youth rally.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during the visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Appearing at his first engagement, he told young people it is "only right" to "acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".

Upon arriving on the island, he met island's Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour on the runway.

The King was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended the island's independence celebrations as Prince of Wales in 1973.

GeneralTab.title: Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises
GeneralTab.text:
Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget.

"The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.

And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change... is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."

So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?

As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), puts it, external: "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints.

"Some of those constraints… are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."

Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything – how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too.

And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.

But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives – a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.

And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high, energy bills are rising and inflation is higher than expected?

In short: it is not easy.

But ministers argue all of this doesn't mean the government is powerless.

Many are expecting support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, to be targeted at the most vulnerable. On the eve of the Budget, Healey said he wants to "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".

The banks are braced for a levy or surcharge that may pay for this.

There will be an announcement about further spending on defence, but not yet how spending 3% of national income on our security will be delivered by 2030 – that will come in next year's Spending Review.

And one of the prime minister's key ideas - handing power away from Westminster and closer to you, devolution - will be central too.

There will be, the chancellor told BBC Newscast, a "really radical devolution of powers and resources to local leaders that are often better placed to get beyond the departmental systems."

But some at Westminster fret extra money for mayors and others in local government are not yet accompanied by adequate checks and balances to ensure that money is well spent.

The chancellor will argue the economy is becoming more robust – and yes, there are some economic indicators that are more positive than forecast: growth is better than expected, as is productivity and unemployment is down.

But as the Resolution Foundation think tank points out, external: "John Healey's problem is that conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates.

"So, despite the signs that the UK economy is becoming more resilient, household and public finances are in for another shock."

In essence, we can expect a smaller Budget this time, compared to some in recent years, when it comes to the scale of tax and spending changes.

The chancellor has been talking up a desire to offer "breathing space" and "hope" - a tacit acknowledgement that there is a limit to what the government can do given the constraints it faces.

It has promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, a self imposed constraint, as the IFS put it. And there are the international ones beyond its control too.

The big question for many will be whether the Budget is – or can be - big enough to meet the moment? Opposition parties will argue it amounts to tinkering.

Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith argued the public finances are "on a cliff edge" and wants Healey to use the Budget to "take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road".

For the Liberal Democrats, Daisy Cooper warned a "steady as she goes" Budget is "not going to cut it", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said the chancellor "can't keep fiddling while the economy burns".

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns wanted a "bold" approach but fears it will be "business as usual".

The government will try to convince you it is one of many moments in the coming weeks and months that will attempt to deliver the scale of change the prime minister has promised.
